Use this when a date slips and you need to know which activities can move without delaying completion.
Build a network of dependencies with durations. Compare path lengths and calculate early and late dates to identify float. Recalculate as actual progress changes.
The instructor emphasizes identifying the longest dependent path and determining float from early and late dates.
Use on predictive schedules or the fixed dependency network within a hybrid project. An adaptive team's flow metrics answer different questions.
A long activity is not automatically critical. Look at its path through the network.
Schedule compression: fast tracking and crashing
overlap activities|add resources to shorten schedule
Use this when the finish date needs to move earlier and removing scope is not an option under consideration.
Compare overlapping critical activities with adding resources to shorten them. Assess the rework risk or extra cost, check approval authority and recalculate the critical path after the change.
The instructor stresses that compressing work away from the critical path will not advance the overall finish unless the schedule logic changes.
Apply to dependency-based scheduling in predictive or hybrid work. In adaptive work, reconsider what can fit in the release instead of assuming overlap improves delivery.
Fast tracking overlaps work; crashing adds resources, usually at a cost. Neither is the same as dropping scope.
Use this when stakeholders need a reliable comparison between intended and actual dates.

Approve a schedule benchmark, collect actual progress, and investigate differences before proposing action. Communicate the forecast separately from the approved baseline and use formal control for baseline changes.
The course emphasizes recognizing why and when a benchmark is approved, then distinguishing measurement from approval to revise it.
Use a baseline on predictive commitments and fixed hybrid milestones. Adaptive teams may track a release forecast separately from governed dates.
Updating the current schedule is not the same as replacing the approved baseline.
Cost estimation, budgeting and funding limits
cost baseline|contingency reserve|funding limit reconciliation|blended team rate|budget at completion
Use this when estimated costs need to fit funding available in particular periods.
Build estimates from the work or the team's expected cost. Check when funds are available, reconcile the spending plan against those limits, and distinguish risk contingency from ordinary estimates.
The instructor calls out funding limit reconciliation and compares estimating by individual resource with using a blended team rate.
Predictive budgeting can aggregate activity costs. Adaptive planning may use a blended team rate. Hybrid can use both where appropriate.
An approved total budget does not mean the full amount is available to spend at any point in time.
Earned value, variances and cost forecasts
earned value management|earned value|planned value|actual cost|cost performance index|schedule performance index|estimate at completion|budget at completion
Use this when you need to distinguish progress earned, progress planned and money spent at a reporting date.

At the same reporting date, compare EV with AC for cost and with PV for schedule. CV = EV − AC; SV = EV − PV; CPI = EV / AC; SPI = EV / PV, with nonzero denominators. State the performance assumption behind any estimate at completion.
The instructor uses EV first as a mnemonic and emphasizes identifying which quantity or formula the scenario asks for.
EVM needs a meaningful cost and progress measurement basis. Use it on baselined work where applicable; iteration metrics alone do not supply all EVM inputs.
SPI expresses schedule performance in earned-value terms. It does not tell you the delay in calendar days.
Risk analysis and threat or opportunity responses
risk register|probability and impact matrix|risk response|threat|opportunity|risk owner|trigger
Use this while an uncertain event could affect your objectives and there is time to prepare a response.

Record the uncertainty, rate probability and impact, then focus further analysis on decisions that justify it. Agree a response, owner and trigger. For threats consider mitigation or avoidance; for opportunities consider enhancing or exploiting them.
Classify the uncertainty before selecting a response. A tactic that reduces a threat is not the same as one that increases a potential benefit.
Review risks as plans or backlogs change. Hybrid teams should include risks at the interface between fixed commitments and evolving work.
Risk mitigation is one response, not the name for all responses. A risk can be a threat or an opportunity.
Use this when something has already happened or a team is actively blocked.
Check whether the risk register already names a response or owner. Log the actual issue, assign a next action and review date, and escalate when the team cannot resolve it within its authority.
Session 5 calls out the distinction: uncertainty about a future event belongs to risk reasoning; a problem already present needs issue action.
Predictive teams may use an issue log. Adaptive teams often track impediments where the team sees them; hybrid uses agreed escalation routes across both.
An issue can create new risks. That does not make the issue itself uncertain again.
Baseline change control and backlog decisions
change request|change control board|baseline change|impact assessment|integrated change control
Use this when a request affects approved scope, dates, costs or contract commitments.

Record the request and evaluate impacts before seeking a decision from the appropriate authority. Keep a record of the decision and update approved plans if authorized. Route changes confined to evolving backlog work through the product owner's ordering process.
The instructor compares predictive and adaptive ways of handling a request. Identify whether a baseline or a backlog is affected before choosing the next action.
Predictive work uses formal control for approved baselines. Adaptive work uses backlog refinement within agreed boundaries. Hybrid needs both routes and a clear boundary.
A request is an input to a decision, not approval to implement. Product backlog ordering is not a substitute for contractual approval.
fixed-price contract|cost-reimbursable contract|time and materials|vendor selection|procurement negotiation
Use this when acquiring external work or negotiating a change with a supplier.
Agree requirements and acceptance evidence with procurement. Compare contract types against how clearly work can be defined and where cost risk belongs. Check who may negotiate, approve and sign.
The course compares contract types and describes the PM's input into negotiation. Read the scope certainty and approval authority in the scenario.
A fixed price can fit well-defined work. Adaptive or hybrid arrangements still need a clear contract boundary and a way to handle changes.
Providing delivery input does not give the PM contract-signing authority.
Use this after a supplier delivers, before treating its contract as closed.
Check deliverables and acceptance against the agreement. Work with procurement to resolve outstanding matters, confirm the required closeout actions and retain the records.
Session 5 asks what remains before formal contract closure when some steps have been done already.
Use the applicable contract closeout process regardless of how the team delivered the supplier work.
Shipping everything is not proof of acceptance or administrative closure. Closing a contract is separate from closing the whole project.
Scrum|product owner|Scrum Master|developers|sprint planning|sprint review|sprint retrospective
Use this when you need to know who orders work or which event to use for a feedback conversation.
Keep product ordering with the product owner and enable the team to organize its work. Use a review to inspect the increment with stakeholders and a retrospective to improve how the team works.
The course discusses Scrum roles and events. Do not treat a course remark about who you are on the exam as a universal rule; use the named role in the scenario.
Use Scrum practices for adaptive work in a hybrid project and agree how evidence from reviews reaches stakeholders outside the team.
The sprint review and sprint retrospective answer different questions about the product and how work happens.
Use this when choosing between working in fixed-length periods and pulling new work as capacity opens.

Agree how often stakeholders need usable work or feedback. For flow, make active work visible and avoid starting more than the team can handle. For timeboxed work, use the iteration boundary to plan and inspect progress.
The instructor flags the comparison between on-demand and timeboxed delivery. Identify whether work moves by capacity or a fixed cadence.
Adaptive teams can use flow or timeboxes; hybrid teams should coordinate their cadence with any fixed milestones or release approvals.
A WIP limit constrains active work. It is not a forecast of how much work will be completed.
Use this after a pattern of problems, at an iteration boundary, or while preparing to transfer the work.
Make time to ask what worked and what should change. Record the learning and turn a useful improvement into assigned work; check later whether it helped.
The course highlights how to prepare and facilitate a retrospective and recommends learning from resolved blockers.
Use regular retrospectives in adaptive work; phase reviews and ongoing lessons capture can serve predictive work. Hybrid can use both.
A lessons log preserves observations. Improvement still requires someone to act on them.
Use this when a sponsor needs to know what changed and what is likely to happen next.
Collect current progress and compare with the relevant plan or baseline. State a forecast and its assumptions separately, explain material deviations and flag decisions needed.
The course points out that forecasts need evidence across work areas, not just a schedule reading.
Predictive reports often compare against baselines. Adaptive reviews can supplement reporting with increments and flow indicators. Hybrid joins the two without equating their measures.
Status describes what has happened. A forecast estimates what may happen next.
burnup chart|burndown chart|velocity|throughput|cumulative flow diagram|lead time|cycle time
burn-up|burn-down|CFD|flow metrics|workflow stage|workflow bottleneck|tasks piling up
Use this when a team needs to explain a release forecast or find where work is queuing.
Use burnup to compare completed work with total scope, burndown to see work remaining, and flow views to look for accumulation. Read a trend in context, especially when scope or the team changes.
The instructor contrasts burnup with burndown and cautions learners to read which quantity the chart plots before interpreting it.
Use these measures for adaptive teams or the adaptive workstream in hybrid. They can complement, rather than replace, milestone tracking.
Burnup chart|Burndown chart|Cumulative flow diagram|Kanban board
Velocity and throughput use different units. A burndown change can reflect a scope adjustment rather than a change in completion rate.
Use this when a new law, economic change or other outside event may affect the project.

Scan for external changes and consult the people who track them. Add uncertain effects to risk monitoring. Assess a live impact and route it through the applicable governance, compliance or change process.
The instructor flags tools for assessing the external environment. Separate monitoring a possible regulation from acting on one that applies now.
All approaches need to respond to external constraints. In hybrid, identify whether a new requirement also affects a fixed commitment.
Market or regulatory scanning is different from approving the project's response.
Project artifacts, PMIS and configuration control
project management information system|configuration management|version control|project documents|management plans
Use this when people cannot find the approved artifact, or multiple versions are in circulation.
Decide where plans and registers live, how people see the current approved version, and how to track changes. Use configuration controls for items that need version and change history.
Session 5 emphasizes distinguishing the information system, artifact management and configuration management. The automatic transcript sometimes misrenders PMIS.
Use appropriate controls in a predictive repository, an adaptive toolset or a shared hybrid workspace; keep authority and version history visible.
Project management plan|Project registers|Configuration management plan|Artifact repository
A register tracks items such as risks or stakeholders. A management plan describes how to manage that work. Configuration control is a function, not simply a folder.
Project or phase closure and formal acceptance
Use this when delivery seems finished but approval, archival or handoff is still open.

Review requirements and unresolved items with stakeholders, obtain and record formal acceptance where required, and archive records others will need. Check what remains before closing the phase or project.
The instructor highlights determining what still needs to be done to obtain approval or close the project. Use the sequence and evidence already present in the scenario.
An adaptive review can provide feedback or evidence. Confirm whether separate formal acceptance is required by governance, contracts or transition arrangements.
Internal completion is not stakeholder sign-off. Procurement closeout has a separate contract scope.
Transition to operations and benefits sustainment
Use this when a team is preparing to hand over a deliverable or check whether expected benefits persist.
Plan who will own the result in operations and what training, documentation or support they need. Agree how outcomes will be tracked after project delivery.
The course distinguishes delivering the result from transitioning and sustaining its benefits. Identify who can still act after the project team leaves.
A predictive project can plan a final handover; an adaptive or hybrid project can arrange transition and feedback around releases.
Project acceptance marks a decision about delivery. Benefits may be measured after closure by the receiving organization.
PMP situational reasoning and study practice
scenario reasoning|first action|exam content outline|instructor callout|practice exams
PMP mindset|what should the PM do first|ECO
Use this when reading a study scenario that asks what the PM should do first or next.

Identify the delivery approach, what has already happened and who can decide. Where the facts are unclear, gather context and consult relevant people before choosing action or escalation. Follow mandatory rules when they apply.
Study the applicable Exam Content Outline and practice timed scenarios. Treat key-slide labels and Susanisms as study cues, not guaranteed exam items or universal rules.
Use context: baseline control and backlog refinement can each be appropriate for different scenarios. Avoid treating a memorized slogan as a substitute for the facts.
Exam Content Outline|Practice review notes|Acronym list
A first-step heuristic is not a rule that overrides governance, ethical obligations or immediate needs.
